title: Two workers, two locks, opposite orders
hook: Each waits politely when a lock is taken. Does someone always get to finish?

knows: two tasks can interleave and clash on shared data (two-writers-one-counter)
doesNotKnow: that locks themselves can freeze two tasks for ever when each holds what the other needs
that one agreed lock order prevents it

misconception: If each worker takes the locks it needs and politely waits when one is busy, someone always finishes eventually.
objective: The learner can explain that when P takes A then B and Q takes B then A, some orders leave each holding the lock the other waits for (a circle of waiting, deadlock), and that taking locks in one agreed order prevents the circle.

claims.text: With opposite lock orders, some runs end with both workers waiting for ever: P holds A and waits for B while Q holds B and waits for A (2 of the 4 possible runs); others finish (e.g. P all three steps, then Q).
claims.source: Builder's node enumeration 2026-10-14 of every scheduler choice under the model (take first lock, take second lock, release both; a worker whose next lock is held cannot step): opposite orders give 4 runs, PPPQQQ, PQ (jam), QP (jam), QQQPPP. Demo.tsx play() uses the same model. Small enough to re-run by hand.

claims.text: With opposite orders the jam happens whenever both take their first lock before either takes its second.
claims.source: If P holds A and Q holds B, P's next lock B and Q's next lock A are both held by the other, so neither can step; if either takes its second lock first, it can finish and release. Node enumeration as in c1.

claims.text: When Q also takes A first, whoever gets A can always get B, so no circle can form; one worker may wait for A, then both finish.
claims.source: Same-order model: B is only ever taken by the holder of A, so the holder of A never waits. Builder's node enumeration 2026-10-14: 2 runs, 0 jammed. Demo.tsx 'Take turns' with the toggle on: Q waits for A, then both finish.

claims.text: Each waiting for the other in a circle is what freezes them (deadlock), and taking locks in one agreed order everywhere is a standard cure for deadlock.
claims.source: Coffman, Elphick and Shoshani (1971), 'System Deadlocks', ACM Computing Surveys 3(2): four conditions incl. circular wait; Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts, deadlock chapter (prevention of circular wait by a total order on resources). Derivation: in any cycle of waits some worker holds a later lock while waiting for an earlier one, which one global order forbids. Not opened by the builder; fact-checker to confirm attribution.

claims.text: A worker who finds a lock taken waits until it is released; each worker takes its first lock, takes its second, then releases both.
claims.source: The lesson's model, stated in the question stem and drawn as each worker's three steps. Idealised: no time-outs, no lock stealing (no preemption).

recall.question: Three tasks share locks X, Y and Z. Which rule makes sure they can never all freeze waiting for each other?
options: Every task takes the locks it needs in the same order, X before Y before Z
Every task waits politely when a lock is taken
Every task takes its locks as fast as it can
recall.why: A freeze needs a circle of tasks, each holding a lock the next one waits for. If everyone takes locks in one order, nobody holding a later lock waits for an earlier one, so no circle can form.
